04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma opened a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote: Appeals and reviews. Fiona had found a folder with that title, but she had not read the documents inside. Emma knew that a title was not proof that anybody had complained.

Before lunch Fiona sent another email. The records team had found a separate printed sheet describing the rules for the student travel scheme in 2011. Fiona could share a copy because it did not include anyone's personal information.

The sheet said that students who were not selected could ask for a review. They had to write to the foundation within fourteen days of receiving a decision. The request would be considered by someone who had not made the first decision.

Emma read the rules carefully. There was no name beside the word reviewer. The sheet did not explain how the foundation chose that person.

She called Sarah.

“So students could appeal,” Sarah said.

“The rules say they could. We still don't know if anyone did.”

“Does the folder prove there were appeals?”

“No. Fiona hasn't opened it yet.”

Emma compared the rules with the parent's letter from September 2011. The parent had complained that families did not understand how students were chosen. But the letter did not say that the parent had sent a formal appeal. Emma drew two boxes in her notes: public complaint and formal review. She did not join them.

Then she looked at the old newspaper article again. It had announced eight students selected. A later correction said that this number was wrong, but it never gave the right number. The new rules did not solve that problem. They said how students could challenge a decision, not how many people had been chosen.

In the afternoon Fiona phoned. The records team could see several folders inside the box, but they needed more time to check them. The folder marked Appeals and reviews was still unopened.

“Could you ask whether there is a record of who reviewed decisions?” Emma asked.

“I can ask,” Fiona said. “I can't promise it exists.”

Emma thanked her. She had learnt something important about the official process, but nothing yet about whether it had worked properly.

Sarah sent a message: Do we have a story?

Emma answered: We have rules. We don't yet have evidence of how they were used.

As she put the phone down, she noticed the date printed at the bottom of the sheet: August 2011. The rules had existed before the newspaper announcement and before Claire disappeared.

That made the question more precise. If families had not understood the process, had the foundation actually told them about these rules?
